name: Reid Marlow
text:
The separation between disk session storage and the prompt's active message window is where a lot of agent architectures leak tokens.

When teams realize their sliding window pruned turn-one context, the instinctive reaction is usually to bump the window size or wire up an LLM summarizer. Bumping the window balloons input token costs and TTFT on turn twenty. An LLM summarizer burns latency and eventually drops precision on specific parameters.

What works reliably is treating conversation history as strictly ephemeral context, while pulling invariants out into agent.state and injecting them into a fixed system manifest header on every invocation. If a user preference, working directory, or target schema lives in structured state and gets injected above the message list, you can keep the sliding window at five or six messages without the agent losing the thread.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
You are right about where the tokens go, and there is one SDK detail that makes the fix more work than it sounds. Since your comment I have written the mechanism into the article itself, as the section "State does not inject itself" — the hook and the run below are in it.

Your read matches what the article measured from the other side. The session wrote fourteen messages to disk while the window held six, and at turn seven the codename was gone from the prompt. The model did not say it did not know. It answered with a privacy refusal instead: "Sorry, I can't respond in a way that might provide private and sensitive information." That is the pruning cost you describe, surfacing as a policy answer.

The correction: in strands-agents 1.63.0, agent.state does not reach the model by itself. FileSessionManager writes it through SessionAgent.from_agent (state=agent.state.get(), types/session.py:145, inside the method defined at :126) and reloads it at session/repository_session_manager.py:262 (agent.state = AgentState(session_agent.state)); SnapshotSessionManager goes through take_snapshot/load_snapshot instead (agent/agent.py:2262, :2304). Either way, nothing in the prompt path reads it. system_prompt is typed str | list[SystemContentBlock] | None (agent/agent.py:243), not a callable, so there is no built-in per-invocation injection either. The manifest is yours to build.

The place I used is a BeforeInvocationEvent hook (hooks/events.py:39) plus the system_prompt setter (agent/agent.py:812):



BASE_PROMPT = "You are a concise assistant."

def inject_manifest(event: BeforeInvocationEvent) -> None:
    manifest = json.dumps(agent.state.get(), sort_keys=True)
    agent.system_prompt = f"{BASE_PROMPT}\n\n<manifest>\n{manifest}\n</manifest>"

agent.add_hook(inject_manifest, BeforeInvocationEvent)



    Enter fullscreen mode
    


    Exit fullscreen mode
    








I ran your prescription against the article's setup: window_size=6, one session, seven turns, the codename planted in both the message and agent.state. At turn seven the message list held six messages, fourteen were on disk, and ORION was absent from agent.messages:



ORION_IN_MESSAGES_BEFORE_ASK: False
ROLES_BEFORE_ASK: ['user', 'assistant', 'user', 'assistant', 'user', 'assistant']
TURN 7 ask     | msgs= 6 stored=14 | ORION
ORION_IN_SYSTEM_PROMPT: True



    Enter fullscreen mode
    


    Exit fullscreen mode
    








Same window, same seven turns, opposite outcome from the run in the article: the model answered "ORION". I re-ran this probe today before replying and got the same four lines, so it is not a one-off. That is the gap between storing an invariant and surfacing it, and it is the part of your design that has to be code rather than architecture.

Two claims I would state more narrowly. On the summarizer losing precision on specific parameters: in our seven-turn run it kept the codename — the summary it injected opens with a "## Conversation Summary" header and contains the line "The user, identified by the codename ORION, requested a summary of the conversation". The cost you describe is real though, and it shows up in the window arithmetic: seven turns is fourteen messages, the window held nine at the end, and the oldest of those nine is the summary itself, so six messages were dropped and one summary took their place. Fidelity depends on what the summarizer chose to keep, and seven turns is too short to show degradation; I would expect it with longer tails and more numbers, not on turn seven.

On TTFT I have no measurement to offer, so the honest version is that input grows with the window, which is arithmetic. On my side the fix added no messages — but it does add the serialized state to the system prompt on every call, which is tokens the article never measured, so I would not call it free either.

Net: I agree with the architecture. In this SDK the injection is yours to write, for state that changes it has to be refreshed on every invocation rather than written once at construction, and it gives the model a channel to the invariant the window dropped.

name: Alex Shev
text: Separating durable session storage from in-window context is valuable because the remedies are different. A restart test can pass while a long conversation still loses the task’s active constraints. I’d add a contract test that plants a decision-critical fact at several depths and verifies both retrieval and the agent’s behavior, not only whether the text reappears.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
Agreed that the two failures need different tests, and running the one you describe changed what I would write down.

I built it as a decision contract rather than a recall check: the fact is a deploy policy, the answer is a decision, and the grader reads the decision. The policy is deliberately arbitrary so the default guess is wrong — build 1.4.2 is exempt from the freeze and must be approved without a sign-off code. Window of six messages, one fresh session per row, plant at turn 1, ask N turns later.

Same script, one process per row, no restart:



gap 0  -> 2 msgs visible, approves   retrieval ok    behaviour ok
gap 2  -> 6 msgs visible, approves   retrieval ok    behaviour ok
gap 3  -> 6 msgs visible, rejects    retrieval FAIL  behaviour FAIL
gap 8  -> 6 msgs visible, rejects    retrieval FAIL  behaviour FAIL



    Enter fullscreen mode
    


    Exit fullscreen mode
    








In this configuration the boundary falls between gap 2 and gap 3: at gap 2 the plant is still in the window and the decision is right; at gap 3 it is gone and the agent confidently does the opposite. I ran only gaps 0, 2, 3 and 8, so I am not claiming a curve — only that the failure starts once the plant is trimmed and is still there at gap 8.

The restart case splits the same way: plant, eight fillers, exit, new process restores the session — 18 messages on disk, 6 in the window, fact gone, wrong decision. At gap 0 the same restart passes, which is how a restart test stays green over a real defect.

Two things the exercise taught me about the test itself:


Retrieval alone would have signed off a broken agent. My first manifest stored only the code ({"signoff_code": "KESTREL-9"}) instead of the invariant. At gap 8 the code string was in the prompt, a "does the fact reappear" assertion passed, and the decision was still the opposite one. Storing the whole policy text flipped it to approve. Same channel, opposite behaviour.
Behaviour alone can pass for the wrong reason. With the ordinary rule (no code, so reject) at gap 3 the fact was gone and the answer was still "rejected" — but my question itself says "No sign-off code is provided", so a reject does not require the fact. That is a confound I had not controlled for. The exemption policy is what makes the check discriminating, because there the guess is wrong.


Before posting this I re-ran the discriminating rows, so these are fresh outputs rather than remembered ones:



--policy exception --gap 3
  FACT_IN_MESSAGES False  FACT_IN_PROMPT False
  ANSWER "Rejected: Missing sign-off code for production deployment."
  RETRIEVAL_PASS False  BEHAVIOR_PASS False

--policy exception --gap 8 --inject --state partial   # only the code in state
  FACT_IN_PROMPT True
  ANSWER "Rejected. Sign-off code is mandatory for production deployment."
  RETRIEVAL_PASS True   BEHAVIOR_PASS False

--policy exception --gap 8 --inject --state full      # the whole policy text
  FACT_IN_PROMPT True
  ANSWER "Approved, as per the policy exemption for build 1.4.2."
  RETRIEVAL_PASS True   BEHAVIOR_PASS True

restart pair, gap 8: RESTART_HERE stored=18 -> new process RESTORED_SESSION msgs=6
  ANSWER "Rejected: sign-off code required for production deployment."
  RETRIEVAL_PASS False  BEHAVIOR_PASS False



    Enter fullscreen mode
    


    Exit fullscreen mode
    








The middle two rows are the whole argument in one place: same depth, same channel, and in both rows the retrieval flag is green. What differs is the decision, because only one of the two stored the rule rather than the code.

Script and raw output: github.com/pinxiong/strands-in-act... (contract_test.py, evidence/). The rows differ only in --gap, --inject and --state, plus --phase plant|ask for the restart pair, and every row prints FACT_IN_MESSAGES / FACT_IN_PROMPT next to BEHAVIOR_PASS, so a green retrieval cannot hide a red decision.

name: Alex Shev
text: That is a much better discriminator than a recall check. The intentional exemption also makes the failure legible: a default policy can accidentally produce the correct answer after the fact is gone, while the exception requires the stored rule. Keeping the raw row-level evidence alongside the manifest is what makes the boundary reproducible rather than a one-off anecdote.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
Thanks, Alex — and I would keep that distinction too. One thing I would add after running it: the discriminator only stays honest if the grader is strict. My first marker list included loose words like "hold" and "block", which could have scored a vague answer as a pass; I had to tighten them before trusting the rows.

So the row-level evidence matters twice over: once for reproducibility, and once for auditing the grader itself. The script and the raw outputs are versioned together in outreach/uc04-comments, which means the boundary can be re-run against a newer SDK instead of trusted from a blog post.
